title.en: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

text.en: Ice melts into water and can freeze again. Bread burnt into toast cannot become bread again. Some changes can be reversed and some cannot.

In a physical change no new substance is formed. Melting ice, dissolving sugar, cutting paper and stretching a rubber band are physical changes. Many physical changes can be reversed.
In a chemical change a new substance is formed with different properties. Burning wood, rusting iron, cooking food and souring milk are chemical changes. A colour change, gas bubbles, heat or light can be clues to a chemical change. Look for evidence of a new substance, because some physical changes also show such clues. Many chemical changes are difficult to reverse under ordinary conditions. Reversibility alone does not tell us whether new substances formed.
Rusting needs iron, air and water. We prevent it by painting, oiling or galvanising. Combustion needs fuel, a source of oxygen in common examples, and enough heat for the reaction. We will compare those conditions in a diagram.
Salt can form crystals when some water evaporates from a concentrated salt solution. The solid crystals are the same salt that was dissolved.
Cooking can be useful, while rusting can damage tools. Changes can also take different amounts of time. A fruit can ripen slowly and a pencil can snap quickly.

Draw a clean ice cube beside its puddle. The water particles are still water particles. The change we can see is from solid water to liquid water.
Imagine freezing the puddle again. The water can return to a solid state even if its shape differs from the first cube. Reversing the state does not need to restore the exact shape.
Tear a sheet of scrap paper using your hands. The pieces are still paper, although the sheet will not naturally join itself back together.

board.text: Torn sheet: new shape, same material

text.en: Look at sugar stirred into water. Separate crystals can no longer be seen, but the sugar is spread through the water. It did not disappear from the mixture.
If an example uses salt instead, crystals can appear as water slowly evaporates. Compare the crystals with the starting salt. They are the same material before and after dissolving.

Consider two cups with bubbles shown in a picture. In boiling water the bubbles are mainly water vapour. In some reactions bubbles are a gas that has just formed. The bubbles alone do not decide the type of change.
Evidence matters more than the number of clues. Ask what was in the starting material and what can be identified afterward. That helps you decide whether a different substance appeared.
Compare a clean iron nail with a nail that has a reddish brown coating after time in damp air. The coating has properties different from shiny iron. It is rust.
A matched nail kept dry can give a comparison. If the damp nail develops more rust than the dry one, the observation supports the role of moisture.
Paint and suitable protective coatings can help slow rust by reducing exposure. Galvanising protects iron or steel with a zinc coating.
Use a diagram to name the three conditions that support ordinary combustion: a fuel, oxygen and enough heat. Changing one condition can stop the reaction in the model.
A piece of wood that is merely cut remains wood. A drawing of the same material after burning shows ash, and burning also produces gases. Those products show a different kind of change.
A single event can include more than one kind of change. In a candle diagram, wax near the flame melts. That melting is physical because liquid wax is still wax.
At the same time, vapour from the heated wax burns and forms new substances. The wax changing state and the wax burning can happen in the same example.
Compare cooked fruit browning with a raw fruit being cut into pieces. Cutting changes the shape. Browning can involve substances in the fruit changing into different materials.
Sometimes describing a permanent change is enough for a practical purpose. For a science classification, go one step further and ask if the materials themselves changed.

board.text: Permanent and chemical answer different questions

text.en: Large rocks can wear down gradually. A moving stream can carry pieces downstream. Carrying existing particles away is movement of material, which can be part of erosion.
A hill can also change when substances in rock react with water or air. One place can show both physical breaking and chemical weathering over time.

board.text: Weathering can include both kinds of change

text.en: Useful and unwanted changes can occur in the same area. A stream might carry away fertile surface soil from one place and deposit sediment in another.

board.text: Desirable depends on the effect and place

text.en: Compare a slowly rusting gate with a pencil that snaps quickly. Decide the type of each change from what it produces, then describe their different speeds separately.
Choose a familiar change and explain it with a before-and-after sketch. Name what you started with, what appears afterward and whether you have evidence of a new substance.

problem.en: Why are melting wax and burning wax different kinds of change?

text.en: In melting, solid wax becomes liquid wax.

why.en: Changing the state leaves the material as wax.

text.en: When wax vapour burns, new substances form.

why.en: Formation of new substances is evidence of a chemical change.

prompt.en: How can you tell if a change is chemical?

requiredIdeas.en: Often with gas, heat, colour or smell.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all reversible changes are physical or all irreversible changes are chemical.

points.en: Ordinary combustion needs fuel, oxygen and enough heat.
